case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Department of Health & Rehabilitative Services v. Yamuni
key_cases.holding: Florida's child welfare agency owes a statutory duty of care to prevent further harm to a child once reports of abuse are received, and caseworker investigation and protective-supervision activity is operational-level conduct for which sovereign immunity is waived under section 768.28.
key_cases.relevance: A child's severe injury after repeated reports supported a negligence verdict against the agency.
key_cases.quote: We agree with the district court below that HRS has a statutory duty of care to prevent further harm to children when reports of child abuse are received.

key_cases.case_name: Floyd v. Department of Children & Families
key_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for the Department was reversed in a wrongful death action alleging that its investigator returned a child to a home with a known abuser, because reporting-related statutory immunity does not protect officials who fail to carry out their duty to protect the child.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Florida appellate decision on agency liability after a child's death following a child-protective investigation.
key_cases.quote: it was not intended to protect those who fail to fulfill their duty to protect children

key_cases.case_name: In re Records of the Department of Children & Family Services (Sarasota Herald-Tribune v. Department of Children & Family Services)
key_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Second District
key_cases.holding: A circuit court considering a petition for access to confidential child abuse records must conduct an in camera review before ruling; refusing to inspect the records was an abuse of discretion and the denial of access was reversed.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Florida procedure by which the public obtains records after a child dies or is seriously injured in the system.
key_cases.quote: the circuit court abused its discretion when it failed to conduct an in camera review of the records to which the Herald-Tribune seeks access

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative federal constitutional duty on a state agency to protect a child from violence by a private actor, so the agency's failure to remove Joshua DeShaney was not a constitutional violation.
key_cases.relevance: DeShaney is the reason fatality claims in Florida proceed under state negligence law rather than section 1983.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

key_cases.case_name: Trianon Park Condominium Ass'n v. City of Hialeah
key_cases.holding: Section 768.28 waived sovereign immunity but created no new causes of action; sorting governmental activity into four categories, the Court held there has never been a common-law duty to individual citizens for the enforcement of police-power functions, so the city was not liable for negligent building-code inspection.
key_cases.relevance: A wrongful-death claim after a child fatality survives only if the agency's conduct falls in a category where a duty of care exists, which is the threshold question Trianon Park poses.
key_cases.quote: First, for there to be governmental tort liability, there must be either an underlying common law or statutory duty of care with respect to the alleged negligent conduct.

key_cases.holding: Where sheriff's deputies responded to a 911 call, engaged an unresponsive woman, conducted a safety check and assured others that no ambulance was needed, the undertaker's doctrine imposed a common-law duty of care, and because that conduct was operational rather than discretionary, sovereign immunity did not bar the wrongful-death claim.
key_cases.relevance: Wallace supplies the undertaker's-doctrine route to a negligence-based wrongful-death claim against a government defendant after a death that followed an official safety check.
key_cases.quote: we further hold that the affirmative actions of the deputies involved in this case were operational in nature; therefore, sovereign immunity does not bar the plaintiff-petitioner's negligence-based wrongful-death claim
